newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Alumbrera mine set for July start-up.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Alumbrera mine set for July start-up.

text.p: Argentina's giant Alumbrera copper mine is set to start up its concentrator before the end of the month, on time to make its first shipments in October, the top project official said Thursday.

Minera Alumbrera Limited project director Shashi Bubna told Reuters that the desert mine in Argentina's northwestern province of Catamarca will start production in the next couple of weeks and pipe out concentrates by mid-August.

"We are pretty much on track with what we were always planning and forecasting and still expect to meet the August 15 concentrator pipeline date. We hope to meet or beat the objective for the first concentrate shipment in October," Bubna said.

Construction of the $1.05-1.1 billion mine is 99-percent complete, with the finishing touches now being put to the concentrates pipeline system, whose design was altered after heavy rains last summer revealed possible risks.
Bajo de la Alumbrera is the first big modern copper mine built in Argentina, and its main partners MIM Holdings say it will be the world's biggest-ever base metal start-up.

Argentina has lured a wave of foreign miners since the government of President Carlos Menem demolished barriers to mining investment in the early 1990s. The government frequently boasts that Argentina controls twice as much territory in the mineral-rich Andes mountains as neighboring mining mecca Chile.

Bubna said that the project had to overcome many problems caused by a lack of infrastructure in the remote site and by an Argentine bureacracy inexperienced in dealing with a project which needed to import 250,000 tonnes of supplies.
But he praised the good will of the authorities, who showed themselves eager to promote the project.

"If they hadn't been enthusiastic we wouldn't have finished the project in less than 26 months," he said, adding that this would have been impossible in a more permit-ridden country like the United States.
"A billion-dollar project in the United States in 26 months?," he said. "No way."

Unusually heavy rains in the summer forced Alumbrera to change plans for pumping its concentrate, and were a major factor in pushing the mine's costs up by at least $147 million from the $903 million estimate last year.
"We built the pipeline and we saw the rainy season, and we did not feel comfortable," Bubna said. "We saw rain and boulders moving."

The initial plan was for a 150-mile (240 km) pipeline to carry the concentrates to a filtration plant in Tucuman province. But Alumbrera is now building a 66-mile (106 km) bypass to eventually join the main pipeline and cut the risk of an expensive accident.
The mine is set to gradually build up to full production over six months, producing an annual average of 180,000 tonnes of copper and 640,000 ounces of gold over 20 years.
Mine work will start with 13 218-tonne Catterpillar trucks, which will gradually be built up to a fleet of 50.
MIM has 50 percent of Alumbrera. Fellow Australian company North Ltd and Canada's Rio Algom Ltd have 25 percent each.
